## From linguistic records to probabilities

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/index/02-concept; notes-page: foundations/index.qmd; note-sha256: 1f31bc7797f38673b1bbe16790dd1d68e0f9632b5625699cdeb601f2022186a7; role: concept -->

Treating any one of these objects as a row produces a different dataset from the same record.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A linguistic record does not determine its own statistical unit. An audio file may contain many word and vowel tokens; a vowel token may in turn contain a duration, a fundamental frequency, and a formant trajectory. Treating any one of these objects as a row produces a different dataset from the same record.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/index.qmd
:::

## From linguistic records to probabilities

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/index/03-concept; notes-page: foundations/index.qmd; note-sha256: 1f31bc7797f38673b1bbe16790dd1d68e0f9632b5625699cdeb601f2022186a7; role: concept -->

A reading-time experiment can retain one row for each trial or average those trials by participant or sentence.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This choice creates the **representation problem (RP)**: before we count anything, we must decide what one row represents and which differences among speakers, items, and tokens remain visible. The same problem arises with every kind of linguistic data. A corpus can be divided into documents, sentences, word tokens, or word types. A reading-time experiment can retain one row for each trial or average those trials by participant or sentence.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/index.qmd
:::

## Linguistic data and comparisons

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/index/06-concept; notes-page: foundations/index.qmd; note-sha256: 1f31bc7797f38673b1bbe16790dd1d68e0f9632b5625699cdeb601f2022186a7; role: concept -->

These facts determine which difference we have estimated.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Second, we turn a research question into a comparison. A numerical contrast is not interpretable until we know which response was measured, how the conditions differed, and whether participants and sentence items occurred in both conditions. These facts determine which difference we have estimated.

## Linguistic data and comparisons

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/index/07-concept; notes-page: foundations/index.qmd; note-sha256: 1f31bc7797f38673b1bbe16790dd1d68e0f9632b5625699cdeb601f2022186a7; role: concept -->

A rank frequency function may describe a corpus well, but that fit does not tell us which process produced the corpus.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Third, we work through Zipf's law by counting word tokens, grouping them into types, ordering the types by frequency, and comparing the observed counts with an inverse rank function. A rank frequency function may describe a corpus well, but that fit does not tell us which process produced the corpus.

## Probability

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/index/08-concept; notes-page: foundations/index.qmd; note-sha256: 1f31bc7797f38673b1bbe16790dd1d68e0f9632b5625699cdeb601f2022186a7; role: concept -->

The outcome definition and the event definition must both follow from the linguistic record and the target comparison.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Now we can state the probability question. What results can the observation process produce, which groupings of those results matter, and how much probability should each grouping receive? A sample space is the set of possible outcomes represented by the model. An event is a set of those outcomes. The outcome definition and the event definition must both follow from the linguistic record and the target comparison.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/index.qmd
:::

## Probability {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/index/09-math; notes-page: foundations/index.qmd; note-sha256: 1f31bc7797f38673b1bbe16790dd1d68e0f9632b5625699cdeb601f2022186a7; role: math -->

The sample space, sigma-algebra, and probability measure form the probability space

$$
\langle\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}\rangle.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We do not always assign probabilities to every subset of the sample space. A sigma-algebra specifies which events are measurable. We construct generated event spaces from attested linguistic features, then define a probability measure that assigns a probability to each measurable event. The sample space, sigma-algebra, and probability measure form the probability space

$$
\langle\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}\rangle.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/index.qmd
:::

## Probability

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/index/10-concept; notes-page: foundations/index.qmd; note-sha256: 1f31bc7797f38673b1bbe16790dd1d68e0f9632b5625699cdeb601f2022186a7; role: concept -->

We conclude with independence: its conditional interpretation is invariance under conditioning, and its unrestricted definition is the product factorization.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Once the probability space is defined, we can calculate probabilities for relations among events. We begin with mutually exclusive events, whose intersection is empty, and introduce the standard comma notation for joint probabilities. We then define conditional probability by restricting probability to a conditioning event. The chain rule follows by rearranging that definition, and Bayes' rule follows by factoring the same joint probability in two orders. We conclude with independence: its conditional interpretation is invariance under conditioning, and its unrestricted definition is the product factorization.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/index.qmd
:::

## Turning linguistic records into data

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/linguistic-data/03-concept; notes-page: foundations/linguistic-data.qmd; note-sha256: 913b54e6b717ad0dfd3aad2fafb1e50e9cfa67c17a3c71daf0867702986ee4bc; role: concept -->

File count does not determine sample size.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

What, exactly, is one datum in an acoustic study? We call the decision that answers this question **unit choice**. A record, such as an audio file, may contain several candidate observations, and several records may contribute to one speaker-level summary. Thus file count does not determine sample size.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872
:::

## Turning linguistic records into data

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/linguistic-data/04-concept; notes-page: foundations/linguistic-data.qmd; note-sha256: 913b54e6b717ad0dfd3aad2fafb1e50e9cfa67c17a3c71daf0867702986ee4bc; role: concept -->

The data record gives the source, preprocessing, license, and checksum.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We make unit choice concrete with Hillenbrand et al.'s (1995) study of American English vowels. The study recorded 45 men, 48 women, and 46 children producing 12 vowels in /hVd/ words, measured duration and formant contours, and asked listeners to identify the intended vowels. The complete teaching table is the audited `phonTools::h95` table from package version 0.2-2.2 under the package's BSD-2-Clause license. One row is one /hVd/ vowel token from one speaker; each speaker contributes one token for each vowel. The package imputed 10 originally missing F2 values and 41 originally missing F3 values, so this table cannot be used to study the release's natural missingness. The data record gives the source, preprocessing, license, and checksum.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872
:::

## Unit and observation key {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/linguistic-data/05-math; notes-page: foundations/linguistic-data.qmd; note-sha256: 913b54e6b717ad0dfd3aad2fafb1e50e9cfa67c17a3c71daf0867702986ee4bc; role: math -->

The pair

$$
\langle\text{speaker ID},\text{vowel}\rangle
$$

is the key in this table.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **unit of observation** is the entity represented by one row. Here it is one vowel token, not one speaker and not one acoustic measurement considered apart from its token. We use **observation key** for the smallest set of columns that identifies a row. The pair

$$
\langle\text{speaker ID},\text{vowel}\rangle
$$

is the key in this table.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872
:::

## The same records, a different question

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/making-sense-of-data/14-concept; notes-page: foundations/making-sense-of-data.qmd; note-sha256: e93aec4503cfd22076a5e8123070a056de2ff101526de2c3bf3e8ac93d81918c; role: concept -->

Shared records do not imply a shared estimand.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The same rows can support at least three distinct questions: (i) how F1 differs between /i/ and /ɪ/, (ii) how duration differs between those vowels, and (iii) whether speakers with larger F1 contrasts also have larger duration contrasts. The first two have acoustic measurements as responses, while the third concerns an association between two speaker-level contrasts. Thus shared records do not imply a shared estimand.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/making-sense-of-data.qmd
:::

## The same records, a different question

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/making-sense-of-data/15-concept; notes-page: foundations/making-sense-of-data.qmd; note-sha256: e93aec4503cfd22076a5e8123070a056de2ff101526de2c3bf3e8ac93d81918c; role: concept -->

None of these failures can be repaired merely by changing the estimator.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Three alignment failures recur in linguistic analysis. First, a token-level dataset may be interpreted as if it contained independent speakers. Second, a predictor may confound the intended contrast with different lexical items or talker groups. Third, evaluation on already observed speakers may be described as prediction for new speakers. None of these failures can be repaired merely by changing the estimator.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/making-sense-of-data.qmd
:::

## A first pattern: Zipf's law

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/03-concept; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: concept -->

We call this dependence the **same-sample rank problem**.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Word types in corpora tend to show a broad inverse relation between frequency and frequency rank. But estimating both quantities from the same counts builds a downward relation into the display. We call this dependence the **same-sample rank problem**.

## A first pattern: Zipf's law

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/04-concept; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: concept -->

We thus carry out an explicitly labeled, paper-aligned replication on UD Turkish BOUN release 2.18, pinned at commit `0def94a229dcbc28d32192b0138b560c075c6d87` under CC BY-SA 4.0.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Piantadosi's (2014) critical review demonstrates the problem with the written American National Corpus, separates rank and frequency estimation by splitting tokens, and shows systematic residual structure beyond a Zipf-Mandelbrot curve. The authorized ANC count snapshot is not available in this repository. We thus carry out an explicitly labeled, paper-aligned replication on UD Turkish BOUN release 2.18, pinned at commit `0def94a229dcbc28d32192b0138b560c075c6d87` under CC BY-SA 4.0.

## A first pattern: Zipf's law

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/05-concept; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: concept -->

The data record gives the checksums and full terms caveat.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Türk et al. (2022) describe the BOUN Treebank and its annotation; Marşan et al. (2022) describe later agglutination-sensitive revisions. The treebank contains written sentences from five Turkish National Corpus registers. Native-speaker linguists manually annotated and cross-checked automatically preprocessed sentences. The prepared table lowercases source surface forms with Turkish dotted and dotless I preserved, and it excludes punctuation, multiword-token range lines, and empty nodes while retaining component syntactic words. One row is one word-form type; `frequency` is its count among non-punctuation syntactic-word tokens. The immediate UD release permits redistribution under CC BY-SA 4.0, though the public documents do not independently expose the upstream Turkish National Corpus permission reported by the paper. The data record gives the checksums and full terms caveat.

[Sources]

## Rank and the descriptive model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/06-math; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: math -->

Let $f(r)$ be the observed token count of the type assigned rank $r$. Zipf's law supplies the basic inverse form

$$
\widehat f(r)
\equiv
Cr^{-\alpha},
\qquad C>0,\ \alpha>0.
$$

## Rank and the descriptive model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/07-math; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: math -->

The Zipf-Mandelbrot generalization shifts rank by $\beta$:

$$
\widehat f(r)
\equiv
C(r+\beta)^{-\alpha},
\qquad C>0,\ \alpha>0,\ \beta\geq 0.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The Zipf-Mandelbrot generalization shifts rank by $\beta$:

$$
\widehat f(r)
\equiv
C(r+\beta)^{-\alpha},
\qquad C>0,\ \alpha>0,\ \beta\geq 0.
$$

The model is a descriptive approximation; matching it does not identify a mechanism of lexical choice, memory, or communication.

## Separate rank and frequency estimation

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/09-concept; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: concept -->

Following Piantadosi (2014), we use a fixed binomial token split.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Following Piantadosi (2014), we use a fixed binomial token split. One count part assigns ranks and the other estimates relative frequency. The random split is a computational device applied to the observed Turkish counts, not a new linguistic dataset. It also does not repair sentence or register dependence because the aggregate table lacks document identifiers.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-014-0585-6
https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/tr_boun/
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-021-09558-0
https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11782
:::

## Separate rank and frequency estimation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/10-math; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: math -->

We fit the curve as a multinomial model over the finite ranked inventory, following Piantadosi's analysis. For $V$ observed word-form types, the model assigns rank $r$ probability

$$
p(r\mid\alpha,\beta)
\equiv
\frac{(r+\beta)^{-\alpha}}
{\sum_{j=1}^{V}(j+\beta)^{-\alpha}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We fit the curve as a multinomial model over the finite ranked inventory, following Piantadosi's analysis. For $V$ observed word-form types, the model assigns rank $r$ probability

$$
p(r\mid\alpha,\beta)
\equiv
\frac{(r+\beta)^{-\alpha}}
{\sum_{j=1}^{V}(j+\beta)^{-\alpha}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-014-0585-6
https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/tr_boun/
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-021-09558-0
https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11782
:::

## Separate rank and frequency estimation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/11-math; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: math -->

If $n_r$ is the frequency-half count at rank $r$, maximizing the multinomial likelihood is equivalent to maximizing

$$
\ell(\alpha,\beta)
\equiv
\sum_{r=1}^{V}n_r\log p(r\mid\alpha,\beta).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $n_r$ is the frequency-half count at rank $r$, maximizing the multinomial likelihood is equivalent to maximizing

$$
\ell(\alpha,\beta)
\equiv
\sum_{r=1}^{V}n_r\log p(r\mid\alpha,\beta).
$$

[Sources]

## Separate rank and frequency estimation

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/12-concept; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: concept -->

Types with zero frequency-half counts remain in the model support even though they cannot appear on a logarithmic plot.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The ranks come from one half and the counts from the other, which removes the same-count error that Piantadosi identifies. Types with zero frequency-half counts remain in the model support even though they cannot appear on a logarithmic plot.

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/zipfs-law/13-concept; notes-page: foundations/zipfs-law.qmd; note-sha256: c0847e2049e14f2b351750a6dcc41b820a90d0933ac2259b26861dfe03b3d22c; role: concept -->

These parameters describe this tokenization of this treebank release; they are not estimates for Turkish as a whole.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The fitted exponent is 0.77 and the fitted rank shift is 0.001. These parameters describe this tokenization of this treebank release; they are not estimates for Turkish as a whole.

The **outcome-representation problem** is the need to decide whether an outcome is a token, a surface form, a lemma, or an annotated lemma-relation combination before assigning probabilities.

[Transcript]

We sample one annotated interrogative-pronoun token from a finite corpus extract. What, exactly, can happen? ## Sample spaces

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/possibilities-and-events/03-concept; notes-page: foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd; note-sha256: 34e64dfacf6b24429b3aaf97e688c24185875bb6308548473326428a9608727b; role: concept -->

This finite extract contains 167 tokens.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We use the UD Turkish BOUN source introduced on the Zipf page. The teaching extract retains tokens whose annotated lemma is *hangi* ‘which’, *kim* ‘who’, or *ne* ‘what’ and whose Universal Dependencies relation is `nsubj` or `obj`. One row is one annotated token nested in a sentence. The preparation filters source annotations and adds binary indicators; it does not infer filler-gap dependencies or recode relations. This finite extract contains 167 tokens.

## Outcomes and the sample space

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/possibilities-and-events/04-concept; notes-page: foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd; note-sha256: 34e64dfacf6b24429b3aaf97e688c24185875bb6308548473326428a9608727b; role: concept -->

The **sample space** $\Omega$ is the set of all such outcomes.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, an outcome is one represented result, and a sample space collects every result the probability experiment allows. More specifically, an **outcome** is one possible result represented by a probability model. The **sample space** $\Omega$ is the set of all such outcomes.

[Sources]

https://universaldependencies.org/u/dep/nsubj.html

We keep token outcomes because the empirical measure on later pages counts rows while retaining the sentence and register identifiers that reveal dependence.

Changing granularity changes the sample space. If outcomes were lemma types, the space would contain the three observed lemmas. ## Omission and impossibility

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/possibilities-and-events/12-concept; notes-page: foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd; note-sha256: 34e64dfacf6b24429b3aaf97e688c24185875bb6308548473326428a9608727b; role: concept -->

It is not an inventory of every interrogative expression in Turkish.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An omitted outcome is not an impossible linguistic result. The extract excludes interrogatives in relations other than `nsubj` and `obj`, and it excludes other interrogative lemmas. Thus its sample space describes a restricted annotated population. It is not an inventory of every interrogative expression in Turkish.

[Sources]

https://universaldependencies.org/u/dep/nsubj.html

## Omission and impossibility

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/possibilities-and-events/13-concept; notes-page: foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd; note-sha256: 34e64dfacf6b24429b3aaf97e688c24185875bb6308548473326428a9608727b; role: concept -->

Sentences, not isolated tokens, were sampled from five registers, and the treebank is not a probability sample of Turkish usage.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This restriction has a useful consequence and a serious limit. It gives a transparent finite experiment for probability calculations, but it licenses only statements about uniform sampling from the retained extract. Sentences, not isolated tokens, were sampled from five registers, and the treebank is not a probability sample of Turkish usage.

## Events

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/events/02-concept; notes-page: foundations/events.qmd; note-sha256: fb0561564cfdf89ba52e2b005d07478246efc7661fbe5affbf7db8c35574f9ea; role: concept -->

We represent such a question by collecting all token outcomes that make its answer “yes.”

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Most linguistic questions do not ask which exact token was sampled. They ask whether that token has a property. We represent such a question by collecting all token outcomes that make its answer “yes.”

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

## Events

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/events/03-concept; notes-page: foundations/events.qmd; note-sha256: fb0561564cfdf89ba52e2b005d07478246efc7661fbe5affbf7db8c35574f9ea; role: concept -->

Once a sigma-algebra $\mathcal F$ has been specified, the measurable events are exactly its members.

::: {.notes}

$$

\equiv

$$

## Sigma-algebras {.section-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/event-spaces/01-section; notes-page: foundations/event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: e99d3ca2c32e10d1dfd1d38b9837e12f492bacc7daa3b094bfe707ba5c73080c; role: section -->



::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The next topic is Sigma-algebras.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces
:::

## Sigma-algebras

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/event-spaces/02-concept; notes-page: foundations/event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: e99d3ca2c32e10d1dfd1d38b9837e12f492bacc7daa3b094bfe707ba5c73080c; role: concept -->

We call this requirement the **closure problem**.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If a model assigns a probability to the event that a token has lemma *ne*, which other events must it measure? It must include the complement, and it must keep unions of measurable events available. We call this requirement the **closure problem**.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces
:::

## Sigma-algebras

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/event-spaces/03-concept; notes-page: foundations/event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: e99d3ca2c32e10d1dfd1d38b9837e12f492bacc7daa3b094bfe707ba5c73080c; role: concept -->

More specifically, a **sigma-algebra**, also called an event space, is a collection $\mathcal F$ that contains the sample space and is closed under complements and countable unions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, we solve the closure problem by collecting events in a way that never strands us without a required complement or union. More specifically, a **sigma-algebra**, also called an event space, is a collection $\mathcal F$ that contains the sample space and is closed under complements and countable unions.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces
:::

## A one-generator event space {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/event-spaces/04-math; notes-page: foundations/event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: e99d3ca2c32e10d1dfd1d38b9837e12f492bacc7daa3b094bfe707ba5c73080c; role: math -->

The sigma-algebra generated by $N$ is

$$
\mathcal F_N
\equiv
\sigma(N)
=
\{\varnothing,N,N^c,\Omega\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The sigma-algebra generated by $N$ is

$$
\mathcal F_N
\equiv
\sigma(N)
=
\{\varnothing,N,N^c,\Omega\}.
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces
:::

## A one-generator event space

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/event-spaces/05-concept; notes-page: foundations/event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: e99d3ca2c32e10d1dfd1d38b9837e12f492bacc7daa3b094bfe707ba5c73080c; role: concept -->

This event space can represent whether the lemma is *ne*, but it cannot distinguish *hangi* from *kim* inside $N^c$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

It contains exactly the unions of the two atoms $N$ and $N^c$. This event space can represent whether the lemma is *ne*, but it cannot distinguish *hangi* from *kim* inside $N^c$.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces
:::

## Closure requirements {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/event-spaces/06-list; notes-page: foundations/event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: e99d3ca2c32e10d1dfd1d38b9837e12f492bacc7daa3b094bfe707ba5c73080c; role: list -->

A collection $\mathcal F$ is a sigma-algebra only if:

1. $\Omega\in\mathcal F$;
2. If $B\in\mathcal F$, then $B^c\in\mathcal F$;
3. If $B_1,B_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F$, then $\bigcup_iB_i\in\mathcal F$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A collection $\mathcal F$ is a sigma-algebra only if: $\Omega\in\mathcal F$. if $B\in\mathcal F$, then $B^c\in\mathcal F$. if $B_1,B_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F$, then $\bigcup_iB_i\in\mathcal F$.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces
:::

The impossible event follows from the first two requirements:

$$
\Omega^c=\varnothing\in\mathcal F.
$$

::: {.notes}

$$

Intersections follow from complements and unions by De Morgan's law:

$$
B\cap C=(B^c\cup C^c)^c.
$$

Intersections follow from complements and unions by De Morgan's law:

$$
B\cap C=(B^c\cup C^c)^c.

## Generators and atoms {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/generating-event-spaces/05-math; notes-page: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: 65e54748d9f64b426ec841288987cc451c57200c6f7162bb475d85696b5f9e06; role: math -->

The generating collection is

$$
\mathcal C
\equiv
\{H,K,N,S,O\}.
$$

Because the three lemma events partition $\Omega$ and the two relation events partition $\Omega$, the nonempty atoms are the intersections

$$
A_{\ell,r}
\equiv
\{\omega\in\Omega:L(\omega)=\ell,\ R(\omega)=r\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $H$, $K$, and $N$ be the lemma events for *hangi*, *kim*, and *ne*, and let $S$ and $O$ be the relation events for `nsubj` and `obj`. The generating collection is

$$
\mathcal C
\equiv
\{H,K,N,S,O\}.
$$

Because the three lemma events partition $\Omega$ and the two relation events partition $\Omega$, the nonempty atoms are the intersections

$$
A_{\ell,r}
\equiv
\{\omega\in\Omega:L(\omega)=\ell,\ R(\omega)=r\}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/generating-event-spaces/06-concept; notes-page: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: 65e54748d9f64b426ec841288987cc451c57200c6f7162bb475d85696b5f9e06; role: concept -->

Each union is included because closure requires it, not because it corresponds to a familiar linguistic label.

::: {.notes}

The empirical cross-classification yields 6 nonempty atoms. Their unions form 64 events in $\sigma(\mathcal C)$. Each union is included because closure requires it, not because it corresponds to a familiar linguistic label.

## Coarser generators

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/generating-event-spaces/08-concept; notes-page: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: 65e54748d9f64b426ec841288987cc451c57200c6f7162bb475d85696b5f9e06; role: concept -->

Adding the three-way lemma partition refines the space again into the observed lemma-by-relation cells.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A generator that records only whether the lemma is *ne* produces the two atoms $N$ and $N^c$. It cannot separate *hangi* from *kim*. Adding the object event refines those atoms into the four cells shown on the preceding page. Adding the three-way lemma partition refines the space again into the observed lemma-by-relation cells.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd

## Coarser generators {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/generating-event-spaces/09-list; notes-page: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: 65e54748d9f64b426ec841288987cc451c57200c6f7162bb475d85696b5f9e06; role: list -->

This gives a finite construction procedure:

1. List the distinctions supplied by the generators;
2. Intersect each distinction with the others and their complements;
3. Discard empty intersections;
4. Take every union of the remaining atoms.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This gives a finite construction procedure: list the distinctions supplied by the generators. intersect each distinction with the others and their complements. discard empty intersections. take every union of the remaining atoms.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd
:::

## When a generator adds no distinction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/generating-event-spaces/11-math; notes-page: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: 65e54748d9f64b426ec841288987cc451c57200c6f7162bb475d85696b5f9e06; role: math -->

If $T$ is the certain event $\Omega$, then adding $T$ to the generating set splits no atom:

$$
\sigma(\mathcal C\cup\{\Omega\})
=
\sigma(\mathcal C).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $T$ is the certain event $\Omega$, then adding $T$ to the generating set splits no atom:

$$
\sigma(\mathcal C\cup\{\Omega\})
=
\sigma(\mathcal C).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd
:::

## When a generator adds no distinction

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/generating-event-spaces/12-concept; notes-page: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: 65e54748d9f64b426ec841288987cc451c57200c6f7162bb475d85696b5f9e06; role: concept -->

What matters is whether the new event divides at least one existing atom.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Likewise, adding an event already expressible as a union of the existing atoms does not enlarge the sigma-algebra. What matters is whether the new event divides at least one existing atom.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd
:::

## When a generator adds no distinction

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/generating-event-spaces/13-concept; notes-page: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: 65e54748d9f64b426ec841288987cc451c57200c6f7162bb475d85696b5f9e06; role: concept -->

It does not license claims about unrepresented interrogative lemmas, non-core relations, or Turkish usage outside the sampled treebank registers.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The generated event space preserves only the distinctions named by the generators. It does not license claims about unrepresented interrogative lemmas, non-core relations, or Turkish usage outside the sampled treebank registers.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd
:::

## When a generator adds no distinction

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/generating-event-spaces/14-concept; notes-page: foundations/generating-event-spaces.qmd; note-sha256: 65e54748d9f64b426ec841288987cc451c57200c6f7162bb475d85696b5f9e06; role: concept -->

Generators determine the finest distinctions a probability measure can express.

## Probability measures

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/02-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: concept -->

We call this requirement the **coherence problem**.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The sample space $\Omega$ specifies token outcomes, and the sigma-algebra $\mathcal F$ specifies measurable groupings. We now need a numerical assignment that does not contradict those objects. We call this requirement the **coherence problem**.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## Probability measures {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/03-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

Basically, a probability measure assigns a number between zero and one to every measurable event. More specifically, a **probability measure** is a function

$$
\mathbb{P}:\mathcal F\rightarrow[0,1]
$$

that satisfies the probability axioms below.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, a probability measure assigns a number between zero and one to every measurable event. More specifically, a **probability measure** is a function

$$
\mathbb{P}:\mathcal F\rightarrow[0,1]
$$

that satisfies the probability axioms below.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## Probability measures {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/04-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

The triple

$$
\langle\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb{P}\rangle
$$

is a **probability space**.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The triple

$$
\langle\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb{P}\rangle
$$

is a **probability space**.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

## The empirical measure {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/05-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

The declared probability experiment samples one token uniformly from the finite extract. For every measurable token event $E$,

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(E)
\equiv
\frac{|E|}{|\Omega|}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The declared probability experiment samples one token uniformly from the finite extract. For every measurable token event $E$,

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(E)
\equiv
\frac{|E|}{|\Omega|}.
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## The empirical measure {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/06-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

Thus every token singleton has mass $1/|\Omega|$, and a linguistic event receives the sum of the masses of its member tokens. For the *ne* event $N$,

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(N)
=
\frac{1}{|\Omega|}
\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\mathbf 1\{L(\omega)=\textit{ne}\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus every token singleton has mass $1/|\Omega|$, and a linguistic event receives the sum of the masses of its member tokens. For the *ne* event $N$,

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(N)
=
\frac{1}{|\Omega|}
\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\mathbf 1\{L(\omega)=\textit{ne}\}.
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## The three requirements {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/08-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

First, every event has nonnegative probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B)\geq 0
\qquad\text{for every }B\in\mathcal F.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

First, every event has nonnegative probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B)\geq 0
\qquad\text{for every }B\in\mathcal F.
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## The three requirements {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/09-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

Second, the full sample space has probability one:

$$
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Second, the full sample space has probability one:

$$
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1.
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## The three requirements {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/10-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

Third, probabilities add across a countable collection of pairwise disjoint events:

$$
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcup_iB_i\right)
=
\sum_i\mathbb{P}(B_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Third, probabilities add across a countable collection of pairwise disjoint events:

$$
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcup_iB_i\right)
=
\sum_i\mathbb{P}(B_i).
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

## The three requirements

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/11-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: concept -->

Their empirical masses thus sum to one, as the calculation verifies.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The six lemma-relation atoms are nonnegative, disjoint, and exhaustive in this extract. Their empirical masses thus sum to one, as the calculation verifies.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

## Consequences of the axioms {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/12-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

The impossible event has probability zero. Since $\Omega$ and $\varnothing$ are disjoint and $\Omega\cup\varnothing=\Omega$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)
=
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)+\mathbb{P}(\varnothing),
$$

so

$$
\mathbb{P}(\varnothing)=0.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The impossible event has probability zero. Since $\Omega$ and $\varnothing$ are disjoint and $\Omega\cup\varnothing=\Omega$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)
=
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)+\mathbb{P}(\varnothing),
$$

so

$$
\mathbb{P}(\varnothing)=0.
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## Consequences of the axioms {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/13-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: math -->

Likewise, $B$ and $B^c$ are disjoint and exhaustive:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1,
$$

and thus

$$
\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1-\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Likewise, $B$ and $B^c$ are disjoint and exhaustive:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1,
$$

and thus

$$
\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1-\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## Counts are not probabilities

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/14-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: concept -->

This transformation changes the scale while preserving relative mass.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The six raw category counts are data-derived nonnegative values, but assigning them directly as event probabilities violates normalization because their sum is the number of tokens rather than one. Dividing every count by the common total produces the empirical mass in the stated identity. This transformation changes the scale while preserving relative mass.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## Probability measures: answer 4

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-measures/24-answer; notes-page: foundations/probability-measures.qmd; note-sha256: 92cf6ff62f6f2708fd2cfc9c7fe51e328405afcb31eb59e1b3a346a8704cf134; role: answer -->

The raw *ne* count is 147, which is not normalized to $[0,1]$; division by the common total gives the empirical probability $147/167=0.880240$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The raw *ne* count is 147, which is not normalized to $[0,1]$; division by the common total gives the empirical probability $147/167=0.880240$.

[Sources]

## Relations among events

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/02-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: concept -->

The distinction is structural: two events may be **mutually exclusive**, **exhaustive**, both, or neither.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Whether event probabilities can be added directly depends on how the events overlap. The distinction is structural: two events may be **mutually exclusive**, **exhaustive**, both, or neither.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd
:::

## Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/03-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: math -->

Events $B$ and $C$ are mutually exclusive exactly when

$$
B\cap C=\varnothing.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Events $B$ and $C$ are mutually exclusive exactly when

$$
B\cap C=\varnothing.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd
:::

## Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/04-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: math -->

They are exhaustive exactly when

$$
B\cup C=\Omega.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

They are exhaustive exactly when

$$
B\cup C=\Omega.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd
:::

## Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/05-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: math -->

Countable additivity thus gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(S\cup O)
=
\mathbb{P}(S)+\mathbb{P}(O)
=1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Within this extract, the `nsubj` event $S$ and the `obj` event $O$ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive because every retained token has exactly one of those two source relations. Countable additivity thus gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(S\cup O)
=
\mathbb{P}(S)+\mathbb{P}(O)
=1.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd
:::

## Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/06-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: concept -->

The *hangi* and *kim* lemma events share no token, but their union excludes the *ne* tokens observed in the same extract.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Mutual exclusivity does not imply exhaustivity. The *hangi* and *kim* lemma events share no token, but their union excludes the *ne* tokens observed in the same extract.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd
:::

## Overlapping events {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/07-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: math -->

The *ne* event $N$ and object event $O$ overlap. For arbitrary events,

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cup C)
=
\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)-\mathbb{P}(B\cap C).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The *ne* event $N$ and object event $O$ overlap. For arbitrary events,

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cup C)
=
\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)-\mathbb{P}(B\cap C).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd
:::

## Overlapping events

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/08-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: concept -->

The subtracted term repairs the double count of outcomes in the intersection.

::: {.notes}

The subtracted term repairs the double count of outcomes in the intersection.

## Overlapping events

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/09-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: concept -->

Adding the two marginal probabilities without subtracting the intersection would exceed the probability of their union by exactly that amount.

::: {.notes}

## Dependence on the outcome representation

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/11-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: concept -->

Changing the unit changes the event relation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Mutual exclusivity is relative to what one outcome represents. If one outcome is one retained token, the two relation labels are mutually exclusive. If one outcome were a sentence, the events “the sentence contains an `nsubj` interrogative token” and “the sentence contains an `obj` interrogative token” could co-occur. Changing the unit changes the event relation.

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-concepts/12-concept; notes-page: foundations/probability-concepts.qmd; note-sha256: 0539dc49240f1b69d6b3c2262d1281192b46154fc4e67ee881c1af1b718e2dda; role: concept -->

The source's annotation schema tells us whether the coded values can co-occur.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Labels alone do not guarantee mutual exclusivity. The *ne* event is a lemma property, whereas the object event is a syntactic-relation property, so one token may belong to both. The source's annotation schema tells us whether the coded values can co-occur.

## Joint probability {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/joint-probability-of-events/02-math; notes-page: foundations/joint-probability-of-events.qmd; note-sha256: fa2f5c2355eeba453ba6d31c2dbc3d0a091f063f85ee1c7eaa568acca150fc29; role: math -->

The probability that two properties hold of the same sampled token is a **joint probability**. For the *ne* event $N$ and object event $O$, we write

$$
\mathbb{P}(N,O)
\equiv
\mathbb{P}(N\cap O).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The probability that two properties hold of the same sampled token is a **joint probability**. For the *ne* event $N$ and object event $O$, we write

$$
\mathbb{P}(N,O)
\equiv
\mathbb{P}(N\cap O).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/joint-probability-of-events.qmd
:::

## Joint probability

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/joint-probability-of-events/03-concept; notes-page: foundations/joint-probability-of-events.qmd; note-sha256: fa2f5c2355eeba453ba6d31c2dbc3d0a091f063f85ee1c7eaa568acca150fc29; role: concept -->

The comma is shorthand for intersection, not an ordering claim: $\mathbb{P}(N,O)=\mathbb{P}(O,N)$.

::: {.notes}

The comma is shorthand for intersection, not an ordering claim: $\mathbb{P}(N,O)=\mathbb{P}(O,N)$.

## The four joint events {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/joint-probability-of-events/04-math; notes-page: foundations/joint-probability-of-events.qmd; note-sha256: fa2f5c2355eeba453ba6d31c2dbc3d0a091f063f85ee1c7eaa568acca150fc29; role: math -->

The two binary distinctions partition $\Omega$ into

$$
N\cap O,
\quad
N\cap O^c,
\quad
N^c\cap O,
\quad
N^c\cap O^c.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The two binary distinctions partition $\Omega$ into

$$
N\cap O,
\quad

\quad
N^c\cap O,
\quad

$$

## The four joint events {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/joint-probability-of-events/05-math; notes-page: foundations/joint-probability-of-events.qmd; note-sha256: fa2f5c2355eeba453ba6d31c2dbc3d0a091f063f85ee1c7eaa568acca150fc29; role: math -->

Their probabilities sum to one because the four events are disjoint and exhaustive:

$$
\mathbb{P}(N,O)
+\mathbb{P}(N,O^c)
+\mathbb{P}(N^c,O)
+\mathbb{P}(N^c,O^c)
=1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Their probabilities sum to one because the four events are disjoint and exhaustive:

$$
\mathbb{P}(N,O)
+\mathbb{P}(N,O^c)
+\mathbb{P}(N^c,O)
+\mathbb{P}(N^c,O^c)
=1.
$$

## Marginal probabilities {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/joint-probability-of-events/06-math; notes-page: foundations/joint-probability-of-events.qmd; note-sha256: fa2f5c2355eeba453ba6d31c2dbc3d0a091f063f85ee1c7eaa568acca150fc29; role: math -->

A **marginal probability** sums over the other distinction. For instance,

$$
\mathbb{P}(N)
=
\mathbb{P}(N,O)+\mathbb{P}(N,O^c),
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(O)
=
\mathbb{P}(N,O)+\mathbb{P}(N^c,O).
$$

::: {.notes}

A **marginal probability** sums over the other distinction. For instance,

$$

## Conditional probability

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/conditional-probability/02-concept; notes-page: foundations/conditional-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 28ad6638496791b76359b6ffe96ef4bcc786d2190340d1742bf623e25806321c; role: concept -->

The phrase *among the* changes the reference event.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The joint probability $\mathbb{P}(N,O)$ is computed relative to the full token extract. Suppose instead we ask: among tokens whose lemma is *ne*, what proportion are annotated `obj`? The phrase *among the* changes the reference event.

## Conditional probability {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/conditional-probability/03-math; notes-page: foundations/conditional-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 28ad6638496791b76359b6ffe96ef4bcc786d2190340d1742bf623e25806321c; role: math -->

More specifically, for events $B,C\in\mathcal F$ with $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, the **conditional probability** of $B$ given $C$ is

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
\equiv
\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, conditioning keeps only the mass inside a reference event and rescales it to sum to one. More specifically, for events $B,C\in\mathcal F$ with $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, the **conditional probability** of $B$ given $C$ is

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
\equiv
\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Conditional probability

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/conditional-probability/04-concept; notes-page: foundations/conditional-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 28ad6638496791b76359b6ffe96ef4bcc786d2190340d1742bf623e25806321c; role: concept -->

The denominator identifies the reference event; the numerator identifies the part of that event for which the target event also occurs.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The denominator identifies the reference event; the numerator identifies the part of that event for which the target event also occurs.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

## Conditioning as rescaling {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/conditional-probability/05-math; notes-page: foundations/conditional-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 28ad6638496791b76359b6ffe96ef4bcc786d2190340d1742bf623e25806321c; role: math -->

Let $N$ be the *ne* event and $O$ the object event. Then

$$
\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(O,N)}{\mathbb{P}(N)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $N$ be the *ne* event and $O$ the object event. Then

$$
\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(O,N)}{\mathbb{P}(N)}.
$$

The empirical value is 0.762. The conditional complement follows from the same rescaling:

$$
\mathbb{P}(O^c\mid N)
=
1-\mathbb{P}(O\mid N).
$$

## Conditioning as rescaling {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/conditional-probability/07-math; notes-page: foundations/conditional-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 28ad6638496791b76359b6ffe96ef4bcc786d2190340d1742bf623e25806321c; role: math -->

Conditioning also makes its own reference event certain:

$$
\mathbb{P}(C\mid C)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Conditioning also makes its own reference event certain:

$$
\mathbb{P}(C\mid C)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=1.
$$

## Three-event and general chain rules {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-factorization/11-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-factorization.qmd; note-sha256: cc2da46c89bae69e57ca37f2b2e27a77bd048432efbb6ffe522fcd0240d8d606; role: math -->

For events $B,C,D\in\mathcal F$, with the displayed conditioning events having positive probability, first write

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)
=
\mathbb{P}(D\mid B,C)\mathbb{P}(B,C),
$$

then factor the remaining joint probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For events $B,C,D\in\mathcal F$, with the displayed conditioning events having positive probability, first write

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)
=
\mathbb{P}(D\mid B,C)\mathbb{P}(B,C),
$$

then factor the remaining joint probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

## Three-event and general chain rules {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-factorization/12-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-factorization.qmd; note-sha256: cc2da46c89bae69e57ca37f2b2e27a77bd048432efbb6ffe522fcd0240d8d606; role: math -->

Substitution yields

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)
=
\mathbb{P}(B)
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)
\mathbb{P}(D\mid B,C).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Substitution yields

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)
=

\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)
\mathbb{P}(D\mid B,C).
$$

## Three-event and general chain rules {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/probability-factorization/13-math; notes-page: foundations/probability-factorization.qmd; note-sha256: cc2da46c89bae69e57ca37f2b2e27a77bd048432efbb6ffe522fcd0240d8d606; role: math -->

Repeating the same move gives the general chain rule:

$$
\mathbb{P}(E_1,\ldots,E_M)
=
\mathbb{P}(E_1)
\prod_{i=2}^{M}
\mathbb{P}(E_i\mid E_1,\ldots,E_{i-1}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Repeating the same move gives the general chain rule:

$$
\mathbb{P}(E_1,\ldots,E_M)
=
\mathbb{P}(E_1)
\prod_{i=2}^{M}
\mathbb{P}(E_i\mid E_1,\ldots,E_{i-1}).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: foundations/probability-factorization.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/02-concept; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: concept -->

The **conditional-direction problem** is that one cannot be read directly from the other.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The probability that a retained *ne* token is an object and the probability that a retained object token has lemma *ne* reverse the target and reference events. The **conditional-direction problem** is that one cannot be read directly from the other.

## Bayes' rule {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/03-math; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: math -->

Recall the two chain-rule factorizations:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Recall the two chain-rule factorizations:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Bayes' rule {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/04-math; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: math -->

The left sides name the same intersection, so

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The left sides name the same intersection, so

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Bayes' rule {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/05-math; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: math -->

If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, divide by $\mathbb{P}(C)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)}
{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, divide by $\mathbb{P}(C)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)}
{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Bayes' rule

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/06-concept; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: concept -->

No independence assumption is used.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This identity is **Bayes' rule**. It reverses the conditional direction while correcting for the two marginal probabilities. No independence assumption is used.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Reversing the empirical conditional {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/07-math; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: math -->

Let $N$ be the *ne* event and $O$ the object event. Bayes' rule gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)\mathbb{P}(N)}
{\mathbb{P}(O)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $N$ be the *ne* event and $O$ the object event. Bayes' rule gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)\mathbb{P}(N)}
{\mathbb{P}(O)}.
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Evidence and prevalence

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/10-concept; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: concept -->

All three quantities are tied to the same finite observation process.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

In this calculation, $\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)$ gives the object rate within *ne*, $\mathbb{P}(N)$ gives the prevalence of *ne* in the retained extract, and $\mathbb{P}(O)$ gives the overall object rate. All three quantities are tied to the same finite observation process.

## Evidence and prevalence

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/11-concept; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: concept -->

Reading the right side of the conditioning bar first identifies the denominator.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The two conditionals may be numerically close or far apart depending on the margins. Their difference is not paradoxical: the shared intersection is divided once by the size of $N$ and once by the size of $O$. Reading the right side of the conditioning bar first identifies the denominator.

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

## Evidence and prevalence

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/bayes-rule/12-concept; notes-page: foundations/bayes-rule.qmd; note-sha256: 7ce3f659e2397649fcd979a4636a9e0ca90871f191cc4da46f43fbe2352786b8; role: concept -->

Bayes' rule is exact for the empirical measure, but its inputs describe that measure.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A potential worry is that the *ne* prevalence in this extract might be treated as a population prevalence for Turkish. It cannot be. The source sampled sentences within five registers, the analysis further selected three lemmas and two relations, and tokens within sentences are dependent. Bayes' rule is exact for the empirical measure, but its inputs describe that measure.

Events $B$ and $C$ are **independent** exactly when

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).

If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, this condition is equivalent to

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B).

## The observed comparison

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/independence/06-concept; notes-page: foundations/independence.qmd; note-sha256: 9b024c3751163a62169fb0d23a108c6d6859c481f9d2c70f5d79914b1e1f0b55; role: concept -->

The two events are not independent in this finite extract.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The observed joint mass is 0.671, while the product-of-marginals model assigns 0.611. Equivalently, the overall object probability is 0.695, whereas the object probability among *ne* tokens is 0.762. Thus the two events are not independent in this finite extract.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

## Why the characterizations are equivalent {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/independence/07-math; notes-page: foundations/independence.qmd; note-sha256: 9b024c3751163a62169fb0d23a108c6d6859c481f9d2c70f5d79914b1e1f0b55; role: math -->

Suppose $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$. If

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C),
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}\\
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}\\
&=\mathbb{P}(B).
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Suppose $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$. If

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C),
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}\\
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}\\
&=\mathbb{P}(B).
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Why the characterizations are equivalent {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/independence/08-math; notes-page: foundations/independence.qmd; note-sha256: 9b024c3751163a62169fb0d23a108c6d6859c481f9d2c70f5d79914b1e1f0b55; role: math -->

Conversely, if $\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B)$, the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
&=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)\\
&=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Conversely, if $\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B)$, the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
&=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)\\
&=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).
\end{aligned}
$$

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Independence is not mutual exclusivity

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/independence/12-concept; notes-page: foundations/independence.qmd; note-sha256: 9b024c3751163a62169fb0d23a108c6d6859c481f9d2c70f5d79914b1e1f0b55; role: concept -->

Independence means that conditioning does not change probability; mutual exclusivity means that co-occurrence is impossible.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If two positive-probability events are mutually exclusive, then their joint probability is the impossible-event probability while their marginal product is positive. They are thus dependent. Independence means that conditioning does not change probability; mutual exclusivity means that co-occurrence is impossible.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Independence is not mutual exclusivity

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/independence/13-concept; notes-page: foundations/independence.qmd; note-sha256: 9b024c3751163a62169fb0d23a108c6d6859c481f9d2c70f5d79914b1e1f0b55; role: concept -->

The empirical table shows dependence in the represented extract and nothing stronger.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Observed dependence also does not identify a causal relation. The association between lemma and dependency relation may reflect the syntactic and semantic distribution of the lemmas, the selected registers, sentence clustering, and annotation choices. The empirical table shows dependence in the represented extract and nothing stronger.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Independence is not mutual exclusivity

<!-- generated-slide-id: data-and-probability/independence/14-concept; notes-page: foundations/independence.qmd; note-sha256: 9b024c3751163a62169fb0d23a108c6d6859c481f9d2c70f5d79914b1e1f0b55; role: concept -->

Changing the corpus population or observation process may change that property.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Independence is a property of events under a particular probability measure. Changing the corpus population or observation process may change that property.

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
